newsitem.title: USA: Bad publicity in Simpson case good for shoe firm.
newsitem.headline: Bad publicity in Simpson case good for shoe firm.

text.p: Lending truth to the Hollywood adage there is no such thing as bad publicity, the Bruno Magli company says sales have soared since its designer shoes were first mentioned in the O.J. Simpson murder case.
With the sensational 1995 criminal trial and Simpson's current civil trial, the Italian shoemaker has received the kind of public exposure money can't buy.
And for 1995-96, Bruno Magli's sales increased nearly 30 percent worldwide, company spokeswoman Jill Eisenstadt said on Wednesday.

"If the trial has contributed, it's that a lot more people are aware of the brand than four or five years ago," said Eisenstadt, of the New York public relations firm, Loving & Weintraub, which handles U.S. publicity for Bruno Magli.

Simpson was acquitted of the June 12, 1994, murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman by a criminal court jury in October 1995. He is now battling a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims.
Simpson said in a sworn pre-trial deposition for his current civil trial that he never owned such "ugly-ass" shoes.
The imported Italian leather shoes have a distinctive sole pattern which investigators say matches a bloody size-12 footprint at the murder scene.
FBI expert William Bodziak, who testified at both trials, said the style of shoe worn by the killer sells for about $160 a pair and only 299 pairs were ever sold in a size 12.

In recent testimony at the civil trial, Robert Groden, a photographic analyst called by the defence, branded a photograph of Simpson wearing Bruno Magli shoes a fake. But photos by another photographer of Simpson apparently wearing the distinctive footwear at the same event were introduced at the trial on Monday.

As 30 new photographs were shown, along with blown-up portions showing the shoes, Groden was asked by plaintiffs' attorney Peter Gelblum if they changed his mind about the earlier photograph being a fake.
"No," he answered repeatedly. But later he said, "If I was able to authenticate these photographs it probably would."

Daniel Petrocelli, the lead lawyer for the plaintiffs, told Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki he would authenticate the new photos "through the defendant, no less, when we confront him with them." Simpson is due to take the witness stand later in the week when he is called by the defence.
Regardless of the outcome of the civil trial the Bruno Magli brand name has become well-known.
"A lot of people have asked us if there's a direct connection between the trial and sales ... we like to think we make good shoes," Eisenstadt said.
The company recently signed a new designer and launched a new advertising campaign with new photographers and models.
Eisenstadt described the 60-year-old firm that makes men's and women's shoes and speciality leather goods as "a very wholesome, family-owned business nestled in the hills of Bologna."

"They don't want to be associated with a heinous crime like a double murder, but they realise the exposure has resulted in name recognition," she said. "Actually, it's not such a big deal up in the hills of Bologna. They know about it, but it's not the same big story as in the United States."
So what of Simpson's less-than-complimentary description of Bruno Magli shoes?
"Who cares what he said? We make good shoes," Eisenstadt replied.
